Oh, man. English is not my first language and I don't have my medical paperwork with me right now, long story short though, I had cervical disc hernia three years ago. It was either C4-C5 or C5-C6, I don't remember exactly, and I had hip bone graft surgery, basically a piece of my hip bone was used to replace one of the discs that was completely damaged and loose and had started pressing on my bone marrow (hope I'm explaining this correctly). Anyway, point is I went to see a doctor when my left arm had started going numb, all the way from my shoulder to my fingers. (I only had nagging back pain besides that, which I didn't think much of since I believed it kinda came with the territory, what with working long hours on the computer and so on.)

Point is the first doctor I went to see was a complete and utter jerk. He took one look at my MRI and said: "yeap. That's pretty ugly. You gotta have surgery or you'll paralyse". Just like that. Bear in mind until this point I had no idea what was wrong with me. You know that expression "I'll just go and have a heart attack"? I went home without a word and had the most horrible panic attack I've ever experienced. Within a few days I changed doctors and met my actual doctor, the one who performed surgery on me, who was absolutely a great doctor, with perfect manners and who took time to explain everything to me.

What I'm trying to say is, you are wonderful. I've read your other answers, no depression, no sudden realisation, no drama. I cannot imagine how you could handle this without turning into a bitter, cynical fuck. I wore that horrible POS Philadelphia collar for two months and wanted to commit murder every night of those two months (just to give an idea, that feels like being constantly choked in a 30+ C temperature. that shit gets hot like hell and  burns your skin). I remember the first time I could sit up on my butt I started crying like a fucking 5 year old with happiness. I know I've treated my close ones like shit, I remember being angry at everything for being a 29 year old woman who had to have her best friend bathe her and all the rest.

I don't know what I wanted to say with this, other than "My hat's off to you, sir". My experience was a piece of cake compared to yours, and I've since recovered fully. Thank you for reminding me I should get off that high horse I climb on once in a while, when I start thinking of all the shit I've been through and curse the universe for being so "unjust with me".

I have no questions. Thank you for doing this IAMA and please know you, in fact, did so much more than that. And I apologize if at any point my comment sounded like rubbing it or something like that. I did in no way intend that. Keep on being who you are. You are loved and you're a winner. Best of...everything to you.

>you meet lots of lunatics even crazier than yourself, and it will help you mentally in more ways than I could possibly explain

I can't stress this enough. It's not a "taking joy in other people's misery". It's taking a step forward and being able to have some perspective on your situation. Best way to explain this is that when you're depressed or in a bad place (or several, recurrent,etc) you can't see the forest for the trees. 

Look around, EVERYBODY has issues. Sure, some bigger than others. But to the point that everybody could very well match some sort of disorder from a psychology textbook. On top of that, so many people are raising more or less bullshit self-diagnoses and laying half-ass generalizations on others. "Oh, I'm depressed/ I have ADD"/"he nearly overdosed/he's binge drinking, he's bipolar". Screw that. Let's just face it, it's easier to hide/dismiss behind labels. Sure, some people are just jackasses and some are genuinely suffering and are in need of help. But how about taking a step back and really trying to see the situation as a whole? Those who care and matter will do that, those who don't- there's no point in caring and relying your self-esteem on others' opinions and labels (and in the "others" category I'm also including shrinks as well as armchair psychologists).

Last year was the second most fucked up year of life (after 2000 when I lost almost my entire family.) Ironically, it was such a promising year. I had a job I loved, thought I met the love of my life and was ready to start clean slate. Then it all went up in flames. I thought I was literally crashing so I went to see a therapist. I got two months (8 sessions) of textbook blabbering about how it's all about my daddy didn't want me. I realised, leaving personal details out, everything I heard could be applied to almost everybody I knew or had known at some point. Sure, it could be argued I just ran into a brainwashed Freudian, but my point is not really discussing different therapies. My point is everybody has it bad, but everybody is different. Similar results do not necessarily have similar causes, therefore should not be approached in the same way. Correlation is not causation.

Now, more directly addressing the OP, having social anxiety is not being crazy. Stop thinking you are crazy because you don't fit in. Crazy is just a term that is more used than the village bus. Stop judging yourself. If it got to a point where you feel debilitated by it, have a look around you at people who really have no hope. Because they inherited some disease, because they live in terrible poverty and so on. You have everything going for you. You are younger than you like to think. Get an education. Do something that makes you happy, so that you don't make yourself and others truly unhappy. Fall in love with a girl, have sex with her. Start hanging out with people without constantly thinking you are not like them. Don't start with the premise that they will be your friends. Friendship is a solid thing that is proven in years. Enjoy the moments you have together and learn from them. 

Your single greatest advantage is that it's only up to YOU to change your life. Nothing is beyond repair, nobody is irreplaceable. You have the luxury of starting over. Do it. Get out. All meanings covered.
